summary: In Greek mythology, Xanthus (Ancient Greek Ξάνθος, "yellow" or "fair-haired") son of Phaenops was a Trojan warrior, twin brother of Thoön. Diomedes kills both brothers in Iliad 5, leaving their aged father without other sons — a miniature tragedy inside the aristeia.
etymology: Xanthos (Ξάνθος) means "yellow" or "fair hair"; the name is shared by river-gods, horses, and many mortals, so the Phaenopid patronymic fixes this node.

sections.heading: Sons of Phaenops
paragraphs: Homer (Iliad 5.152–158) sends Diomedes after Xanthus and Thoön, sons of Phaenops, both well beloved. Their father is fordone with grievous old age and begets no other son to leave in charge of his possessions; Diomedes bereaves him of both in one rush of fighting.

sections.heading: Homonyms
paragraphs: This node (xanthus-phaenopid) is the Trojan Phaenopid. Distinct from Scamander (the gods' name Xanthus), Achilles' immortal horse, Hector's horse, the Theban king Xanthus son of Ptolemy (xanthus-theban), Sarpedon's supposed father in some Lycian notices, and the many other golden-named figures on the Wikipedia list.
